A misspelled id leaves an orphan alias that will never be shown anywhere, and the successful-looking response is identical to the one a correct id produces. Copy the id from the machine list rather than typing it.

tools.name: update_machine

tools.description: List machines (active wardens): machine_id/display_name/online.
tools.name: list_machines

tools.description: Bootstrap on server: runs `ocwarden install --force` on the SERVER's own host. machine_id is NOT a target — this verb has no way to reach another machine, and naming one is refused (409); the server-local machine is the only value it accepts, and the install overwrites the existing one, which is how you repair this host's warden. To install a different machine, fetch that machine's own boot command with GET /api/machines/{machine_id}/boot-command and run it on that host.

machine_id.description: Which machine the caller claims to be talking about — NOT a target selector. The install always happens on the server's own host: the child process is addressed by the server's HOME and uid, never by this parameter. An unknown or retired id is a 404; the server-local machine (its id is 'm-server-self') is the one value that proceeds, and it reinstalls this host's warden with `install --force`, overwriting an existing install rather than refusing. Every OTHER id that resolves is a 409, refused before anything is installed or written, because honouring it would put this host's warden under another machine's identity. There is no flag that widens this verb: to install a different machine, fetch that machine's own one-liner with GET /api/machines/{machine_id}/boot-command and run it on that host.

tools.name: install_warden_on_server_host

tools.description: Teardown on server: runs `ocwarden teardown` on the SERVER's own host. machine_id is NOT a target — this verb has no way to reach another machine, and naming one is refused (409). The server-local machine is refused too (retiring it revokes credentials fleet-wide). To retire another machine use uninstall_machine then delete_machine; to repair the server host's own warden use install_warden_on_server_host, which runs `install --force` over the existing install.

machine_id.description: Which machine the caller claims to be talking about - and today no value gets past the guard. An unknown or retired id is a 404; every id that resolves is a 409, in one of two ways, and the two refusals do NOT tell you the same amount. Naming the server-local machine (its id is 'm-server-self') answers one bare sentence - the server-local machine cannot be deleted - with no route to try instead. Naming any OTHER machine answers a long refusal that DOES name the way out, because this verb carries no machine selector at all: it can only ever tear down the warden on the server's own host, so honouring the request would destroy this host's daemon under another machine's name. That second message is the one that points at the remote uninstall plus a delete to retire another machine, and at install_warden_on_server_host, which runs install --force to repair this host. Read it even when you meant the first one: the repair path for THIS host is only ever printed there.

tools.name: uninstall_warden_on_server_host

tools.description: Uninstall a machine: drive the uninstall RPC to its warden.
tools.name: uninstall_machine

tools.description: Upgrade a machine: kick its warden's self-update NOW.
tools.name: upgrade_warden

tools.description: Delete a machine: soft-delete its warden record (no command sent).
tools.name: delete_machine

tools.description: Read the user-custom additive context block (empty = is_default).
tools.name: get_global_context

tools.description: Whole-block replace of the user-custom additive block ({text}). text is REQUIRED; unknown keys are rejected. Replacing existing content with an empty block needs allow_shrink=true (or use reset_global_context).

text.description: The ENTIRE global context - the boot instructions every agent in the studio reads - not an addition to it. Sending a fragment answers 200 and permanently drops the rest, and the blast radius is the whole roster: every agent that boots after this write reads what you sent and nothing else. Read the current text first and fold your change into it. NOTE THE GUARD ASYMMETRY: emptying a document that had content is refused unless allow_shrink is set, but this document has NO CHARACTER CAP at all, so there is no upper bound and no refusal for a write that is merely far too long, or far too short without being empty.
text.title: Text

tools.name: replace_global_context

tools.description: Reset the user-custom block to empty (idempotent tombstone).
tools.name: reset_global_context

tools.description: List role definitions (seed defaults + owner edits) WITHOUT the persona bodies: each row is the role identity plus its definition size and cap, never definition_md itself. Read the one role you want with get_role.
tools.name: list_roles

tools.description: Size-only overview of EVERY capped document on the station: each role's role definition / insight / DEFAULT lessons bucket, and each task manual's SOP / learnings, as size_chars plus the cap_chars in force for THAT segment (the five segments have five separate caps — each is reported against its own). LIMITATION: lessons is reported for the default bucket only; nothing stops a write from naming another bucket, and such a document spends the same lessons cap yet never appears here. Carries NO document text, so it costs a few hundred bytes. Use it to find which long-lived document is nearly full, then read only that one (get_role / get_insight / get_lessons / get_task_manual). It is the only way to see insight and lessons sizes in bulk — no listing reports those at any price; the manual sizes and caps are also on every list_task_manuals row, and a role definition's size and cap are already on every list_roles row.
tools.name: peek_doc_sizes

tools.description: Create a custom role + its founding member (one pair per call). runtime is claude/codex (absent = claude).

member_name.description: Name for the first member created under the new role. Omitting it is neither an error nor a no-op: the server picks a name from its own pool (avoiding every name the roster has ever carried, removed rows included) and hires that member anyway, 200. Nothing tells you a name was chosen for you - the only place it appears is member.name in the response, so read that back rather than assuming the member is nameless or was not created at all.
member_name.title: Member Name

model.description: Model the new role's member launches with. There is NO model whitelist anywhere in the server: runtime and effort in this same call are checked against closed sets and 422 on anything else, but this string is trimmed and stored exactly as sent. A typo, a retired model name, or a model the chosen runtime cannot launch all answer 200 here and only surface much later, as a member that fails to spawn. Blank is legal and leaves the launcher's own default in place.
model.title: Model

name.description: The ROLE's name - the job, not the person. Blank is refused (422) and nothing else about it is checked, and the mistake this parameter invites is a silent one: put a person's name here and you get a role NAMED after a person plus a member whose own name the server picked out of its name pool, both created, 200. The member's name is member_name; this field is what the role is called. The duty document is not yours to set here either - the new role starts from the standard template and is written afterwards through update_role.
name.title: Name

tools.name: create_role

tools.description: Read one role definition (unknown → 404).
tools.name: get_role

tools.description: Edit a role definition ({name?, definition_md?}; locked names skip).

definition_md.description: Replaces the WHOLE role definition, not an addition to it - a fragment answers 200 and permanently drops the rest. The only guard here is the character cap, and it is one-directional BY DESIGN: it refuses writes that are too long, and never refuses one for being too short. There is no wipe guard on this path, so an empty string is accepted and clears the definition. Read the current text first and fold your change into it.
definition_md.title: Definition Md

name.description: The role's display name - and for a FACTORY role it is SILENTLY DISCARDED rather than refused. The write applies the name only when the role is not one that ships with the product; for a factory role the field is skipped, the rest of the write proceeds, and the response answers 200 carrying the OLD name. Nothing says the rename was dropped, so the only way to know is to compare the name you sent against the name you got back. On roles you created yourself the field behaves as you would expect.
name.title: Name

tools.name: update_role

tools.description: Reset a role definition to seed (idempotent tombstone overlay).
tools.name: reset_role

tools.description: Hard-delete a custom role + its members (seed → 403; online → 409).
tools.name: delete_role

tools.description: Read a per-role insight doc - this role's accumulated judgement calls and trade-offs (per role_key). A role may ship with a factory seed, and that seed is PER-ROLE (seeds/insight_<role_key>.md) - today only the assistant has one; a role without one reads genuinely empty until it writes. is_default=true means THIS ROLE has never written its own, whether what you are reading is the factory wording or nothing at all. Separate from the lessons doc on purpose: lessons record what happened and what to do next time, insight records how this role weighs a call. Like lessons, reading is unrestricted: any authenticated identity may read ANY role's insight - it is SEPARATE, not private.

role_key.description: Names WHOSE insight to read, and an unknown role is NOT an error: measured 2026-08-14, a role_key no role carries answered 200 with text:"", size_chars:0, is_default:true and has_seed:false - byte for byte what a real role that has never written its insight answers. The response echoes back the role_key you sent, and that echo is the only signal available; it confirms what you asked, never that anyone answers to that name. So an empty read is not evidence the role wrote nothing, it is equally evidence you misspelled the role. Confirm the key against the roster before concluding anything from emptiness.

tools.name: get_insight

tools.description: Whole-doc replace of a per-role insight doc ({text}). text is REQUIRED; unknown keys are rejected. Replacing existing content with an empty doc needs allow_shrink=true. Only the role's own agents (and admin) may WRITE it.

role_key.description: Names WHOSE insight this replaces. Nothing checks the key against the roster - it becomes the storage key as sent - so who catches a typo depends on WHO YOU ARE. An ordinary member may only write its own role, so a misspelling is refused with 403. An admin or the owner may write any role, and for them a misspelling silently creates an insight document under a role nobody answers to, complete with its own version history and change notification, and answers 200. The role you meant is untouched and unmentioned.

text.description: The ENTIRE insight doc, not an addition to it. Sending a fragment answers 200 and permanently replaces everything else, so read the doc first and fold your change into it, or use patch_insight to edit by anchor. The two guards here catch only the extremes: emptying a doc that had content needs allow_shrink, and the character cap is enforced. A replace that simply loses most of the text is neither empty nor over cap and passes silently.

tools.name: replace_insight

tools.description: Patch a per-role insight doc by unique anchors ({edits:[{old,new}]}). Only the role's own agents (and admin) may WRITE it.

role_key.description: Names WHOSE insight to edit. Nothing checks the key against the roster, so who catches a typo depends on WHO YOU ARE: an ordinary member may write only its own role and is refused with 403, while an admin or the owner is not refused at all. For them, an edit with a non-empty old fails to find its anchor in an empty document and returns 400, but the APPEND form (empty old) has no anchor to miss - it creates an insight document under a role nobody answers to and answers 200, leaving the role you meant untouched.

tools.name: patch_insight

tools.description: Reset a per-role insight doc back to its factory seed (idempotent tombstone of the overlay) - the counterpart of reset_role on the Duty block. A role with NO seed file (seeds/insight_<role_key>.md) returns 404: there must be a factory version to reset TO. No length cap is applied on this path, matching reset_role - the factory text is part of the product. The overlay you are discarding is retained as a document-history revision, so the reset is recoverable. Only the role's own agents (and admin) may do it.
tools.name: reset_insight

tools.description: Read a per-role lessons doc (per role_key; overlay ⊕ seed).

role_key.description: Names WHOSE lessons to read. Reads are unrestricted and the key is not checked against the roster at all, so a role_key no role carries is not an error: the call answers 200 carrying the factory seed text, which is what a real role that has never written its own lessons also answers. The response echoes the role_key you sent - that echo confirms your input, never that anyone answers to that name. Treat a seed-looking answer as ambiguous between 'this role has written nothing' and 'this role does not exist', and settle it against the roster rather than against this response.

task_type.description: Names WHICH lessons bucket to read, and a name no bucket carries is NOT an error: the call answers 200 carrying the 14-character factory shell, which is indistinguishable from a bucket that exists and has simply never been written. Measured 2026-08-14 against one role: an invented bucket name answered size_chars=14 / is_default=true, while that same role's real bucket answered size_chars=14897 / is_default=false. NEITHER DIRECTION OF is_default SETTLES IT - true does not mean 'this role never wrote one', and false does not mean 'there is content here' (a bucket holding only the 14-character shell reads false). So a short answer is not evidence the role is empty; it is equally evidence you named a bucket that does not exist. Know which bucket names are legal BEFORE you ask - the response cannot tell you afterwards.

tools.name: get_lessons

tools.description: Replace the WHOLE per-role lessons document. text is REQUIRED and unknown keys are rejected; only that role's agent or an admin may write it; emptying or sharply shrinking it needs allow_shrink=true; and the result is still judged against the lessons cap.

role_key.description: Names WHOSE lessons this replaces. Nothing checks the key against the roster - it goes straight into the storage key - so who catches a typo depends entirely on WHO YOU ARE. An ordinary member is saved by authorization: it may only write its own role, so a misspelling is refused with 403 and the mistake announces itself. An ADMIN OR THE OWNER may write any role, and for them a misspelling is not refused at all: it creates a lessons document under a role nobody answers to, answers 200, and fans a delta for it. The role you meant is untouched and unmentioned. The higher your privilege, the quieter this fails.

task_type.description: Names WHICH lessons bucket this whole-doc replace lands in, and NOTHING validates it: the value is used verbatim as half of the storage key (role_key::task_type), so a name no bucket carries does not fail - it CREATES a new document under the misspelled name and answers 200. The bucket you meant is left exactly as it was and is never mentioned; the response echoes the task_type you sent, which is the only signal you get. The wipe guard does not save you, and not for the reason it looks: a bucket nobody has written does not read as empty, it reads as the ONE shared seed file every role falls back to, so writing real content over that seed is not a wipe and the guard passes. OMITTING the field is safe over MCP and is not the same risk - a blank task_type is folded to the default 'general' bucket at the tool boundary. It is a typo, not an omission, that loses the write.

text.description: The ENTIRE lessons doc, not an addition to it. Sending the paragraph you wanted to add answers 200 and permanently drops everything else, so read the doc first and send it back with your change folded in - or use patch_lessons, which edits by anchor. Two guards stand here and neither catches the ordinary version of this mistake: emptying a doc that had content is refused unless allow_shrink is set, and exceeding the character cap is refused. A replace that merely loses most of the text is neither empty nor over cap, so it passes without comment.
text.title: Text

tools.name: replace_lessons

tools.description: Patch a per-role lessons doc by unique anchors ({edits:[{old,new}]}).

role_key.description: Names WHOSE lessons to edit. Nothing checks the key against the roster, so who catches a typo depends on WHO YOU ARE: an ordinary member may only write its own role and is refused with 403, while an admin or the owner may write any role and gets no refusal at all. For them the edit form decides what happens next - an edit with a non-empty old cannot find its anchor in an empty document and fails with 400, but an edit with an EMPTY old (the append form) has no anchor to miss and CREATES a lessons document under a role nobody answers to, answering 200 while the role you meant stays untouched.

task_type.description: Names WHICH lessons bucket to edit, and NOTHING validates it: the value is used verbatim as half of the storage key (role_key::task_type). A name no bucket carries does not fail - and it does not read as an empty document either. What you get back is the ONE shared seed file every role falls back to (a single line of boilerplate), marked is_default: true on get_lessons; that flag is the only thing distinguishing a bucket nobody has written from one that has. What happens next depends on the edit form. A NON-EMPTY old is refused with 400 - whole batch, zero writes - because your anchor is not in that seed line. An EMPTY old (the append form) has no anchor to miss: it appends onto the seed, CREATING a document under the misspelled name, and answers 200 while the bucket you meant stays untouched and unmentioned. OMITTING the field is safe over MCP, but nothing in your client does that for you: it is the SERVER's /api/mcp handler that substitutes the default 'general' bucket for a blank task_type, after your call has arrived and before it re-enters the route. So what actually lands is an ordinary write to 'general' - it is a typo, not an omission, that loses the write.

tools.name: patch_lessons

tools.description: Bounded LIGHT wake snapshot for the caller (identity-locked; recent chat + light open-task rows + size overview — peek sizes first, pull detail via get_task). CHAT is packed newest-first under a CHARACTER BUDGET, not a fixed message count, and stopping at the last message that still fits; each message carries from_name/to_name beside the ids and ts_display (full date + time + zone offset) beside the epoch ts, and folds in its reply card as `card` when it has one — read every ts_display against the top-level `generated_at`. TWO DIFFERENT things can be missing and they are marked DIFFERENTLY: `body_omitted_chars` > 0 means THAT message is here with that many characters COLLAPSED away (another agent's line — the owner's line and your own hand-off notes to yourself are carried in full), re-read it with get_chat; `chat_earlier_omitted` is the other kind and it is a MAYBE, not a fact: that line was cut at a read or budget limit and nothing looked past the cut, so whole messages may be missing from this payload entirely — it is raised even when there is in fact nothing older. Its hint tells you how to CHECK and fetch them. The two are asymmetric ON PURPOSE: the collapse marker is CERTAIN (that message IS here, shortened, exact count); this one is not, and only the fetch settles it. Also carries the STUDIO FLOOR you wake up onto: roster (every member and contractor, each with online/offline status, the machine it runs on, and its duty capped at 1000 chars with `…` marking a cut, the cap applied after the doc's own leading title line is removed — who to ask for help; no insight/learning by owner ruling. Contractors additionally carry their bound task's status, waiting_reason, and step progress (progress_done/progress_total) — members leave these at their zero value; a contractor's 0/0 is ambiguous (a task with no steps yet, or no task at all) and task_status is what tells them apart, non-empty vs empty) and machines (the machine list plus you_are_on, your server-recorded machine binding — never derive it from a hostname). It also carries `doc_capacity` — the long-lived capped documents in your reach that are CLOSE to full (your role documents, the boot documents, your open tasks' manuals, your open steps' notes), each with size/cap, what is left, and whether YOU can rewrite it or have to ask the person who can. The key is ABSENT when nothing is near, so its presence is the whole signal — act on it now, not when a write is refused.
tools.name: resume_summary

tools.description: Size-only PEEK of the wake snapshot (identity-locked; overview counts/sizes + estimated_total_chars, NO chat/task content). estimated_total_chars is exactly chat_chars + tasks_detail_chars + roster_chars + machines_chars + steps_on_answered_card_chars + doc_capacity_chars, all six reported in overview: the WHOLE chat block as the snapshot renders it (chat_chars is the rendered block's cost, NOT the sum of the message bodies), plus the plan text its task rows omit, the two studio-floor blocks, the named steps sitting on an answered card, and the near-cap document rows (0 unless something is close to its cap) — what pulling the snapshot actually costs. Step one of the two-step boot: call this FIRST to size resume_summary, then either call resume_summary directly (small) or hand the pull to a cheap sub-agent that returns a digest (large).
tools.name: peek_resume_summary_size

tools.description: List tasks (?executor=&type=&status=, or statuses=[…] for a SET of states — every filter given is ANDed; LIGHT list items — id/task_no/title/type_key/status/priority/executor/creator_id/progress/timestamps/deps + dep_tasks, WITHOUT steps/description/inputs). Ask for the states you actually want (`statuses: ["not_started", "in_progress"]`) instead of listing everything and filtering yourself — the whole history is a large answer. `statuses` also accepts "reassigning", which matches the handover LOCK rather than the status column. `dep_tasks` already carries each blocker's task_no/title/status, so a blocked task needs no follow-up get_task just to name what it is waiting for. Call get_task for a task's full detail (steps, description, inputs).

executor.description: Filter to one executor. It is a plain string comparison against each task's executor id - nothing resolves it, so an id nobody carries is not an error: you get 200 with an EMPTY list, which is exactly what a real executor with no tasks returns. An empty answer is therefore not evidence that someone has no work; it is equally evidence you misspelled them.
executor.title: Executor

open.description: The literal STRING "true" (not a boolean, and any other value is ignored) drops every task that has already reached a terminal status — done, terminated, duplicated — and returns only the work that is still live. Use it instead of enumerating statuses when all you want is "what is still open"; it composes with executor/type/status. Omitted, the list carries the closed tasks too, which on a long-lived roster is most of it.
open.title: Open

type.description: Filter to one task type. It is a plain string comparison against each task's type_key - no manual is looked up, so a type_key that names no manual answers 200 with an EMPTY list rather than an error, indistinguishable from a real type that currently has no tasks. Take the key from list_task_manuals rather than typing it.
type.title: Type

tools.name: list_tasks

tools.description: Create a task (dedupes on the manual's key; ad-hoc when type_key omitted). Pass target.kind=outsource to drop the task as an unassigned outsource task (發包); target.runtime is claude/codex (absent = claude). The existing outsource scheduler then spawns workers against the global concurrency cap (outsourceParallelCap) — below the cap it starts immediately, at the cap it queues for capacity and is picked up automatically when a slot frees. No owner-approval card and no per-task approval; the owner may reassign a still-queued task at any time. Caller authorization (正職授權矩陣, T-23cf): an outsource worker may never create a task; a 發包 create is open to any 正職 (owner/admin included); a typed task the manual assigns to member X may be created only by X (owner/admin NOT exempt); an ad-hoc task with a member executor may name only the caller itself unless the caller is owner/admin (a 一般正職 may self-execute or 發包, never assign another member).

description.description: The task's body text - what the executor reads to learn what is actually being asked. It is stored exactly as sent, with no validation and no length limit, and omitting it is not an error: the task is created with an empty description and answers 200. Nothing downstream fills it in and title is the only other free text the executor gets, so a task created without this arrives as a one-line instruction to whoever picks it up.
description.title: Description

executor_member_id.description: The member who is to execute the task. It is REQUIRED whenever the task ends up member-executed and the type manual names no assignee (blank is a 400), and it is ignored entirely when the manual assigns the type or when target routes the task to an outsource worker. What it never gets is a roster lookup - the id is stored as given. A plain agent is protected by the rule that it may only name ITSELF (anything else is a 403), so the silent failure belongs to owner and admin-agent callers: a mistyped id creates a task assigned to a member who does not exist, answers 200, and is then executed by nobody.
executor_member_id.title: Executor Member Id

inputs.title: Inputs
inputs.description: The manual's fields, as {field_name: value}. An UNDEFINED field name is NOT dropped: the whole map is stored on the task verbatim and reads straight back out of get_task, and the only thing marking it is one line in the response's warnings[] saying the field is not defined in that manual. So a value under a misspelled name survives, is never read by anything, and a 200 alone will not tell you. Two misspellings are NOT silent, because the field they were meant for is then left with no value: a required field answers 400 'required input ... is missing', and a manual's identifying (is_key) field answers 400 'identity key ... must not be empty' - so a typo cannot slip past dedupe by emptying the key. Matching is case- and space-insensitive, so two names that fold together keep the first in sort order and warn about the other. Ad-hoc tasks (no type_key) have no manual to check against at all: the map is stored unexamined, with no warnings. READ warnings[] on every typed create.

target.description: Dispatch target. The kind is matched as the EXACT string 'outsource' (surrounding whitespace is trimmed, case is not folded): any other spelling - 'outsourced', 'Outsource', a typo - does not fail and is not warned about. The entire target block is discarded and the task is created down the ordinary member path instead, which answers 200 with a perfectly normal-looking task. So a task you meant to put out to a contractor can come back as a task assigned to a member, and nothing in the response says so. Check the created task's executor_kind rather than trusting the create to have read your target. The MACHINE is the other quiet one, and it bites even when the kind is spelled right. Leaving target.machine out is not an error and usually costs nothing: the field is filled from the type manual's outsource assignee, and then from the machine YOU are pinned to as the creator - though an owner-scope caller has no roster row to lend and contributes nothing here. When none of those three names a machine the field simply stays empty: runtime and effort have defaults, a placement deliberately does not, and nothing else invents one. The task is still created with 200 and reads as normal, and the worker minted for it later does not boot at all until somebody names a machine on it - until then it just sits there with a no_machine_selected receipt on the WORKER row, which is the only place this ever surfaces.

tools.name: create_task

tools.description: Read one task (steps, deps, progress, gate cards).
tools.name: get_task

tools.description: Terminate a task — close it as terminated, the only status change that does not go through the task's own step reports. WHO: the owner, an admin agent, or the task's OWN executor when that executor is a 正職 member (T-b56e, owner 2026-08-20 card rc-b896e3f641e7). A member terminating SOMEONE ELSE's task is a flat 403. An OUTSOURCE worker is a flat 403 even on its own task: the task is the reason that worker exists, so self-termination would end it with nobody watching — ask the owner or an admin agent instead. Non-terminal only (already closed → 409).
tools.name: terminate_task

tools.description: Set a task's priority (owner/admin agent any value on any task; the task's own executor any value on their task — frozen INCLUDED, and whoever may freeze may unfreeze, T-6020). The actor who sets frozen is recorded on the task as frozen_by and the field clears when the task leaves frozen. Anyone else is a flat 403. Answers with a bounded receipt (task_id, priority, frozen_by), not the whole task — use get_task when you need the rest.
tools.name: set_task_priority

tools.description: Message the task's executor (owner/admin agent; task context auto-attached).

ChatAttachmentInputDTO.description:
An attachment carried on a posted chat message — either INLINE BYTES or a
REFERENCE to a blob already in the shared attachment store.

Inline: ``data_b64`` is the bytes, base64-encoded — a data-URI
(``data:<mime>;base64,....``) OR bare base64 (the handler strips a
``data:...;base64,`` prefix if present). ``mime`` and ``filename`` are
optional: an omitted ``mime`` is sniffed for images (else
``application/octet-stream``); an omitted ``filename`` defaults for pasted
images.

Reference: ``id`` names an EXISTING blob (minted by
``POST /api/chat/attachments`` — the streaming upload seam that keeps file
bytes out of a JSON tool call). The stored blob's mime/filename are
authoritative: ``filename``/``mime`` sent alongside ``id`` are IGNORED (so
the upload response ``{id, mime, filename}`` can be pasted back verbatim).
An unknown ``id`` is a 400; carrying BOTH ``id`` and ``data_b64`` is a 400
(ambiguous intent). An item with neither ``id`` nor ``data_b64`` is a
400 (T-e2b2: it used to be dropped silently, so a sender that named a file it
never sent got a success and the recipient got nothing). The reply-card ANSWER face is
inline-only: it decodes ``data_b64`` and has never resolved ``id`` references,
so an item carrying only an ``id`` there is a 400 (T-e2b2 — it used to be
dropped silently).
ChatAttachmentInputDTO.title: ChatAttachmentInputDTO

tools.name: post_task_message

tools.description: Submit/replace the workflow plan (done and answered-card steps are kept). T-74f8 交棒閘 (second door): a plan is a step-set write and the task status is DERIVED from the step set, so a plan that leaves EVERY step done CLOSES the task — the same irreversible close the final step report performs. If that task's creator is not its executor and no handover is declared or already real, the replan is refused with 422 BEFORE anything is written (the plan stays fully editable). A plan carries no handoff field, so the way out is to hand over first: create the successor task and point its ``blocked_by`` at this task (the gate then stands aside by itself), or keep one unfinished step and declare the handover on the ``update_step_status`` report that closes it. A replan that still leaves work in the plan is never gated. Answers with a bounded receipt (task_id, steps_total, progress_done, progress_total), not the plan you just sent — use get_task to read the stored step rows back.
tools.name: submit_plan

tools.description: Correct THIS task's own TEXT — its title, its description, or both in one write (T-646a). Replaces `update_task_title` and `update_task_description`, which documented the same rules twice and could not be applied together: changing both meant two calls, two transactions and two SSE deltas, with room for someone else's write to land in between. WHO: the task's own executor, or an admin/owner; anyone else is a flat 403. Creating a task grants NO standing to keep rewriting it — if you handed the task over, it is the new executor's text now. PARTIAL: only the fields you NAME are touched, so omitting a field is a legal no-op for it that versions nothing and fans nothing. ⚠️ THE TWO FIELDS TREAT AN EXPLICIT BLANK DIFFERENTLY, and that is an owner ruling rather than an inconsistency (card rc-796541192519, 2026-08-11, option ①): a blank `title` ("" or whitespace-only) is REFUSED with 400 and does NOT clear the field, because create_task refuses a blank title too and an edit door looser than the create door would let a caller reach a task-list row with nothing in it; a blank `description` IS accepted and DOES clear the text, because plenty of cards legitimately have no prose. VALIDATION IS WHOLE-BODY AND HAPPENS FIRST: a request carrying a blank title alongside a perfectly good description writes NEITHER — a 400 leaves the task exactly as it was, never half-applied. Both values are trimmed of surrounding whitespace before they are stored AND before they are compared with what is there, so re-sending the same text with a stray trailing space is correctly seen as no change rather than spending one of the retained revisions saying nothing moved. ⚠️ THAT HOLDS ONLY WHILE THE STORED TEXT IS ALREADY TRIMMED. Whenever the stored description carries untrimmed whitespace, the next edit here normalises it and therefore DOES spend a revision — even when you re-send exactly what you read back. TWO things can put untrimmed text in that column, so this is not a one-time settling: create_task, which never trims the description (it does trim the title), and a RESTORE of a revision that holds untrimmed text, which is written back verbatim. Before this ticket both doors stored it raw and agreed; this tool trims and create still does not, which is a divergence awaiting a ruling rather than a promise about the system. The write is wholesale within each field: send the full corrected text, not a fragment. ⚠️ Division of labour with update_step_note: the DESCRIPTION says what this task IS (stable); the step NOTE says where a step is RIGHT NOW (volatile, handover-facing) — do not put progress here. A CLOSED task (completed / terminated / duplicated) is STILL editable, on the same terms — unlike its artifact set, which freezes at close: artifacts record what the task PRODUCED and must stop moving, while a ticket worded wrongly is usually found to be wrong after it closed, and freezing the text would preserve a known falsehood in the permanent record. Every change that actually alters a field retains the previous value as a document version — kind `task_title` / `task_description`, key = the task id — so a correction is recoverable through list_document_history and the older wording is never simply gone.

title.title: Title
title.description: The new title, replacing the whole of it. OMITTING the field is a no-op for the title: nothing is written, nothing is versioned, nothing fans, and the call still answers 200 with the task — so the status code alone never tells you whether a rename happened; read the title back if you need to know. A blank or whitespace-only title is REFUSED (400, 'title must not be blank') and takes the WHOLE request down with it, `description` included. ⚠️ Reaching that guard requires the blank to actually arrive: at least one MCP client serializes an empty string as an ABSENT field, which lands in the no-op branch instead (observed four times over, 2026-08-11) — so a caller trying to clear a title may get silence rather than the 400. Surrounding whitespace is trimmed before the value is stored and before it is compared with the current title. Contrast `description` on this same tool, where a blank is a real write that clears the text.

description.title: Description
description.description: The new description, replacing the whole of it. OMITTING the field is a no-op for the description: nothing is written, nothing is versioned, nothing fans. An EMPTY STRING is NOT refused — it is a genuine write that CLEARS the description, which is the opposite of what `title` does with the same input and is deliberate (a card with no prose is a true state; a card with no title is a blank row on the list). Surrounding whitespace is trimmed before the value is stored and before it is compared with the current description, so re-sending the same text with a stray trailing newline is correctly seen as no change. A description that is ONLY whitespace therefore trims to "" and CLEARS.

tools.name: update_task

tools.description: Mark a not-yet-terminal task duplicated, pointing at an existing final original (executor/owner). A blank original, an original that cannot be found, a self-reference, a chained duplicate and a target that is already pointed at are all refused. Closing across executors creates a handoff_follow_up, and no dependency is added.
tools.name: mark_duplicate

tools.description: Report a step status (pending/in_progress/waiting_external/done). Entering waiting_external requires a non-blank waiting_reason (422 otherwise); the task status is derived from its steps. T-74f8 交棒閘: if this report would CLOSE the task (every step done) AND the task's creator is not its executor, the call is REFUSED with 422 unless you say where the ball goes IN THIS SAME CALL — handoff='return_to_creator' (recorded on the task and nothing else — no task is opened and nobody is notified), handoff='follow_up' + handoff_task_id=<a successor task you already created> (the server hangs this task off it as a dependency, and closing this one releases it), or handoff='none' + handoff_note=<why nothing follows>. The gate stands aside by itself when a non-terminal task already depends on this one — you never see it if the handover is already real. It refuses BEFORE writing anything, so a refused report leaves the plan fully editable: create the successor task, then re-send this same report with the declaration. This is your LAST chance — once the task closes it can never be replanned (submit_plan becomes a permanent 409).

handoff.description: Where the ball goes when this report closes the task: 'return_to_creator' | 'follow_up' | 'none'. Read ONLY on the report that would close the task; ignored otherwise.
handoff.title: Handoff

handoff_note.description: The handover sentence. REQUIRED for handoff='none' — an un-reasoned "nothing follows" is indistinguishable from forgetting, and the note is the only record that a decision was made at all.
handoff_note.title: Handoff Note

handoff_task_id.description: The successor task id. REQUIRED for handoff='follow_up'; the server adds this task to that successor's blocked_by list.
handoff_task_id.title: Handoff Task Id

waiting_reason.description: Why this step is blocked on the outside world. It is read ONLY when the status being reported is waiting_external, where it is REQUIRED and a blank one is refused (422). Under EVERY OTHER status the field is not merely ignored - the reason is actively CLEARED, so a report that carries a perfectly good reason alongside, say, in_progress both discards what you sent and erases the reason already recorded, answering 200 either way. Leaving waiting_external is meant to clear it; the surprise is that any other report does too.
waiting_reason.title: Waiting Reason

tools.name: update_step_status

tools.description: Write this step's working note: where the work stands and what comes next — the field the handover SOP means by 「把還在進行中的工作寫回 task step note」. WHAT TO WRITE — three things, then stop: (1) STATE — one sentence on where this step actually got to; (2) NEXT — one sentence on what whoever takes over does next; (3) EVIDENCE POINTERS — version ids, file and log paths, what you verified YOURSELF versus what you are taking on someone's word, and the limits of what was NOT done. Long narrative does not live here: reasoning and scope belong in the task description, reports and diffs belong on the task as artifacts. The note is the current state — not a report, not an append-only log. Writable in ANY step status (pending, in_progress, waiting_owner, waiting_external, done, superseded), unlike `waiting_reason`, which is locked to waiting_external. Wholesale write: `note` replaces whatever was there and "" clears it, so rewrite it as the work moves rather than appending; over 4,000 characters (counted in runes) is refused. Same executor/admin gate as every other task-driving write (403 otherwise). ⚠️ A task auto-closes when its last step is reported done and a closed task 409s — so write the note BEFORE the report that finishes the last step, not after. The receipt carries `size_chars` / `cap_chars`, so the room left is on every write instead of only on the 400 that refuses one; `get_task` reports the same pair per step as `note_size_chars` / `note_cap_chars`.

note.description: The note text. Replaces the step's note wholesale; "" clears it. Write what the next session needs: where this step got to, what is in flight, what comes next.
note.title: Note

tools.name: update_step_note

tools.description: Patch this step's working note by unique anchors ({edits:[{old,new}]}) — send only the part that changed, instead of re-typing the whole note. USE THIS WHENEVER YOU ARE AMENDING A NOTE THAT ALREADY HAS CONTENT. update_step_note is a wholesale replace, so if anyone else wrote to the step between your read and your write, your copy is stale and the replace silently deletes their text — and because your stale copy is usually the LONGER one, no guard fires and nothing tells you. A patch cannot do that: a non-empty old must match the current note EXACTLY ONCE (0 or >1 hits reject the WHOLE batch with a 400 that names which edit failed and which tool to re-read with, zero writes), so a concurrent write turns into a refusal you can see. Edits apply in order; an empty old appends. Wiping the note, or shrinking it below a tenth, needs allow_shrink=true — for an honest rewrite from scratch use update_step_note. Same executor/admin gate, same any-step-status generality, same closed-task 409 as update_step_note. Re-read with get_task after a refusal.
tools.name: patch_step_note

tools.description: Arm a gate step: opens the reply card the owner must answer. Optional attachments ride the question (same shape as post_chat: {id} from `ocagent upload` / POST /api/chat/attachments, or inline data_b64).

ChatAttachmentInputDTO.description:
An attachment carried on a posted chat message — either INLINE BYTES or a
REFERENCE to a blob already in the shared attachment store.

Inline: ``data_b64`` is the bytes, base64-encoded — a data-URI
(``data:<mime>;base64,....``) OR bare base64 (the handler strips a
``data:...;base64,`` prefix if present). ``mime`` and ``filename`` are
optional: an omitted ``mime`` is sniffed for images (else
``application/octet-stream``); an omitted ``filename`` defaults for pasted
images.

Reference: ``id`` names an EXISTING blob (minted by
``POST /api/chat/attachments`` — the streaming upload seam that keeps file
bytes out of a JSON tool call). The stored blob's mime/filename are
authoritative: ``filename``/``mime`` sent alongside ``id`` are IGNORED (so
the upload response ``{id, mime, filename}`` can be pasted back verbatim).
An unknown ``id`` is a 400; carrying BOTH ``id`` and ``data_b64`` is a 400
(ambiguous intent). An item with neither ``id`` nor ``data_b64`` is a
400 (T-e2b2: it used to be dropped silently, so a sender that named a file it
never sent got a success and the recipient got nothing). The reply-card ANSWER face is
inline-only: it decodes ``data_b64`` and has never resolved ``id`` references,
so an item carrying only an ``id`` there is a 400 (T-e2b2 — it used to be
dropped silently).
ChatAttachmentInputDTO.title: ChatAttachmentInputDTO

body.description: The gate's full text - the background, the consequences and the trade-offs behind the approval being asked for. It is stored as sent with NO validation, so omitting it is not an error: the gate opens with an empty body and answers 200, leaving the owner a summary and some buttons with nothing explaining what he is approving. Nothing warns you that it went out empty.
body.title: Body

tools.name: open_gate

tools.description: Replace the blocking-deps list wholesale.
tools.name: set_task_deps

tools.description: Report the task's close-out follow-ups done (terminal tasks only; idempotent).
tools.name: report_task_closeout

tools.description: Reassign a task to a member or a fresh outsource worker (executor-guarded: a plain agent may reassign only a task it executes; owner/admin drive any task). Caller authorization (正職授權矩陣, T-23cf): owner/admin may hand a task to any active member or 發包 it to a fresh outsource worker; a 一般正職 may only turn its own task into a 發包 (a member target is 403); an outsource worker may not reassign at all. An outsource target uses target.runtime claude/codex (absent = claude), lands the task unassigned for the scheduler to spawn under the global parallel cap, and enters the reassigning handover state.

note.description: What the successor needs in order to pick the work up. The only check is a length cap, and a blank or omitted note is not an error - but it is not neutral either: the note is written onto the task ONLY when it is non-blank, so omitting it leaves whatever handover_note an EARLIER reassign put there, still carrying that author and timestamp, sitting on the card as though it described this handover. The takeover message itself is server-authored and goes out either way; your note is simply appended to it when present. On an outsource reassign there is no successor to message yet - the worker has not been minted - so the note reaches the task row only.
note.title: Note

target.description: Where the task goes next. kind is required and must be 'member' or 'outsource' (anything else is a 400) - and the two branches read DIFFERENT sub-fields, which is where this call loses things quietly. member_id is a DECLARED field of target, so strict decoding accepts it under EITHER kind; send it with kind 'outsource' and the outsource branch never reads it, so it simply vanishes - no 422, no warning. The reverse direction is destructive rather than merely lossy: kind 'member' does not just ignore runtime, model, effort and machine, it RESETS the outsource spec already sitting on the task row - runtime back to 'claude', model, effort and machine blanked, the explicit-dispatch flag cleared - and none of those columns appear in any response, so nothing you can read afterwards shows they were ever there. kind 'member' also needs member_id (owner or admin-agent only; the target must be an active, non-outsource, non-warden roster row, and naming the current executor is a 409). kind 'outsource' validates runtime and effort, and resolves machine ONLY when you send a non-blank one - an id that resolves to nothing is a 400 there, but omitting the field is asked nothing at all: it is then filled from the type manual or from you the dispatcher, and when neither of those names a machine either it stays EMPTY, the reassign still answers 200, and the worker minted for the task does not boot until somebody names a machine on it (a no_machine_selected receipt on the worker row is the only trace). It also names no successor: the task lands unassigned and the scheduler mints a worker for it later, under the global cap.

tools.name: reassign_task

tools.description: Take over a reassigned task (the new executor claims it): clears the reassigning lock and fires the predecessor worker. The task status stays derived from its steps; only the lock is cleared. 409 if the task is not under the reassigning lock.
tools.name: claim_task

tools.description: Register a deliverable (file, image, or link) onto the task's artifact set — the pinned deliverables shown on the task card. Append-only and repeatable: call it again to pin more. For a file or image, first upload the bytes via the chat-attachments upload to get an attachment id, then call this with kind=file|image and that attachment_id. For a link (e.g. a PR url) call it with kind=link and url — no upload needed. label is an optional display name (a link title such as "PR #123"). Answers with a bounded receipt (task_id, artifact_id, artifact_count), not the whole task.

url.description: The link target, read ONLY when kind is 'link' - where it IS required, a blank one being a 400. It is never parsed and never fetched: any non-empty string is accepted as sent, so a typo is pinned as a deliverable that leads nowhere. With kind 'file' or 'image' this field is not merely optional but never looked at at all - those artifacts are taken from attachment_id and the url is dropped without a word, so a file artifact sent with a url and no attachment_id is refused for the MISSING attachment_id, not for the field you actually filled in.
url.title: Url

label.description: Human-readable caption for this deliverable. It is stored exactly as sent and never validated - blank, duplicated or wrong, nothing objects - and omitting it is not an error: the artifact is pinned with an empty label and answers 200. What the reader gets then is an untitled row whose only identity is its kind and the file or link behind it, which on a task carrying several artifacts is the difference between a list someone can act on and a list they have to open one by one.
label.title: Label

tools.name: add_task_artifact

tools.description: Un-pin (remove) one artifact from a task's artifact set — the counterpart to add_task_artifact. You may remove artifacts from a task you are the executor of (the owner/assistant may remove on any task). Give the task id and the artifact id (the id returned when it was added, or from get_task's artifacts). The underlying file blob is left intact; only the pin on the card is removed. ONLY WHILE THE TASK IS STILL OPEN: once a task closes (done / terminated / duplicated) its deliverable set is frozen in both directions — remove is refused with the same 409 as add. So swap a deliverable BEFORE you close the task, not after; after the close it can neither be removed nor put back. Answers with a bounded receipt (task_id, artifact_id, artifact_count), not the whole task.
tools.name: remove_task_artifact

tools.description: List live outsource workers (codename, model, effort, task).
tools.name: list_outsource_workers

tools.description: Read an outsource worker's boot-context preview (owner/admin agent).
tools.name: get_outsource_worker_boot_context

tools.description: Refocus (換手) an outsource worker (owner/admin agent, online-only else 409).
tools.name: refocus_outsource_worker

tools.description: Stop (停止) an outsource worker: kill + hold down (owner/admin agent).
tools.name: stop_outsource_worker

tools.description: Restart (重啟) an outsource worker that has no live session (owner/admin agent; 409 only when it is actually alive).
tools.name: restart_outsource_worker

tools.description: Change (換 model) an outsource worker's model/effort (owner/admin agent).

effort.description: Optional effort quick-pick; null/absent keeps the current effort.
effort.title: Effort

model.description: New model for the outsource worker. It is trimmed and stored with no whitelist of any kind - runtime and effort in this same call ARE checked and 422 on an unknown value, and that 422 returns BEFORE the row is written, so a rejected effort also throws away the model you sent alongside it - and a blank string is a legal value meaning the launcher's default, not 'leave it as it is'; to leave it alone, omit the field. The value is persisted before anything else happens, so a 200 says nothing about whether it is usable. Exactly ONE combination is acted on now: status 'active' AND a session that is connected at this moment. An assigned worker, or an active one whose session is not connected, is written to the row and nothing else - it picks the value up at its next spawn. The connected active worker then has THREE outcomes, not two. If the owner has already stopped it (desired_state offline), nothing is started at all: the model is saved and the row is stamped held_down, telling you to restart it when you want it to run. Otherwise the call opens a hand-over window and tells the worker to wind down, and the kill plus respawn on the new model happens when it reports stopped, or when that window's deadline runs out - UNLESS this refocus epoch's wind-down was already collected (its refocus AND stopped anchors both set), in which case the kill and the respawn go out inside this very call. So in the ordinary case an unusable model name does not take the worker down while you hold the 200 - the old model keeps running until the hand-over closes, and only then does the respawn fail.
model.title: Model

runtime.description: Optional runtime replacement; null/absent keeps the current runtime.
runtime.title: Runtime

tools.name: set_outsource_worker_model

tools.description: List task types WITHOUT their long documents: each row is the type identity (type_key / display_name / purpose), its input fields and its assignee setting, plus the SIZES of sop_md and learnings and the cap each is judged against. The SOP and the learnings text are not on this answer at all — read the one type you picked with get_task_manual.
tools.name: list_task_manuals

tools.description: Create a task type: pass display_name; the server mints and returns the tm- type_key id (legacy explicit type_key still accepted; duplicate → 409; assignee = owner/admin agent). An outsource assignee may select runtime claude/codex; absent = claude.

assignee.description: Who executes tasks of this type. Supplying it at all is governance - a caller below admin-agent is a 403 - and the sub-keys the server KNOWS are checked properly: kind must be 'member' or 'outsource' (400 otherwise), an outsource runtime, effort and copies are each validated against their own range, and an outsource machine must actually resolve. What is not checked is anything else you put in the object: unknown sub-keys are neither rejected nor read, just marshalled into the stored blob, so 'copys' or 'mashine' are accepted with 200 and then never take effect. TWO known keys also escape checking, and the second one is the expensive one. member_id is only tested for being non-empty, never looked up in the roster. model is never mentioned by the validator at all - yet it is what a spawn reads, and by two routes: every task this manual itself routes to outsource, AND an explicit target on create_task/reassign_task that left model unset on a task of this type, which inherits this one (the manual's model rides along when the two runtimes agree). So an unusable model name is stored with 200 and surfaces much later as a spawn that fails. A model that is not a string is not refused either: it is dropped as if you had never set it, and the field then falls through to the creator snapshot written on the task row when the task was created, reaching the launcher default only when that is empty too. Compare runtime and effort in this same object, which refuse a value they do not recognise.
assignee.title: Assignee

display_name.description: Human-readable label for the type. Whether a blank one is refused depends entirely on the OTHER field: with no type_key this is the only input there is, so blank is a 400; with a type_key supplied, a blank display_name is silently backfilled with that type_key and answers 200. The failure is therefore not an error message but a type list in which one row is labelled with its raw id while every other row carries a real name.
display_name.title: Display Name

type_key.description: Stable id for the new task type, and the legacy compatibility path: supply it and it is taken verbatim as the id, an existing one being a 409. OMITTING it is not a validation error - the server mints an id of its own ('tm-' plus twelve hex characters) and creates the manual under that, 200 - so a caller who meant to set a memorable key ends up with a random one and finds out only by reading type_key back out of the response. On that minting path display_name becomes mandatory (blank is a 400); on the legacy path a blank display_name is silently backfilled with this key.
type_key.title: Type Key

tools.name: create_task_manual

tools.description: Read one task manual (purpose/fields/SOP/learnings/assignee). The SOP and the learnings are judged by two SEPARATE caps: read sop_md_cap_chars and learnings_cap_chars. The older cap_chars is DEPRECATED — it carries the LEARNINGS cap only and says nothing about sop_md, so read sop_md_cap_chars for the SOP.
tools.name: get_task_manual

tools.description: Edit a task manual (partial; content fields agent-editable; assignee = owner/admin agent). An outsource assignee may select runtime claude/codex; absent = claude. Only the fields you name change, so omitting a field is safe — but unknown keys are rejected rather than dropped: the learnings doc goes in learnings (NOT text — that is write_task_learnings' field name). The SOP and the learnings are judged by two SEPARATE caps: read sop_md_cap_chars and learnings_cap_chars. The older cap_chars is DEPRECATED — it carries the LEARNINGS cap only and says nothing about sop_md, so read sop_md_cap_chars for the SOP.

assignee.description: Replacement assignee object for the type - governance, so a caller below admin-agent supplying it is a 403. It is a WHOLE-OBJECT replacement, not a merge: what you send becomes the entire assignee, so an outsource assignee re-sent as kind plus machine silently drops the copies and effort that were there before, and an empty object clears the assignee altogether. Both answer 200. The same checks as the create face apply - kind must be 'member' or 'outsource', an outsource runtime, effort and copies are range-checked and machine must resolve - and so does the same gap: unknown sub-keys are stored verbatim and never read, and member_id is only tested for being non-empty, never looked up.
assignee.title: Assignee

display_name.description: The manual's human-facing name — what list_task_manuals shows and what people match on when they pick a type — as opposed to type_key, the immutable id you address it by. Pass it to rename a type without breaking anything that references the key (leading/trailing whitespace is trimmed). Omitted leaves the stored name untouched, like every other field on this partial update.
display_name.title: Display Name

learnings.title: Learnings
learnings.description: Replaces the WHOLE learnings doc of this manual - and unlike write_task_learnings, which writes the same document, this path has NO wipe guard. write_task_learnings refuses to empty a doc that had content unless allow_shrink is set; here {"learnings": ""} is simply accepted and answers 200 with the document gone. Only the character cap is checked. Because both calls write the same doc, the safety you get depends purely on which one you happened to use, and nothing in either response says which protections applied. Omit the field to leave the doc alone; send the full current text with your change folded in when you do mean to write. Also note the field names are NOT interchangeable between the two calls: this one is 'learnings', write_task_learnings takes 'text'.

purpose.description: Replaces the manual's whole purpose text. Nothing validates it - no cap, no wipe guard, no format check - so an empty string clears it and a fragment replaces the rest, both answering 200. Omit the field to leave it alone; send the full text when you do mean to write.
purpose.title: Purpose

sop_md.description: Replaces the WHOLE SOP of this manual, and it is the only way in - there is no patch-by-anchor counterpart for this document the way patch_task_learnings exists for the learnings half. The only guard is the character cap: unlike write_task_learnings, there is NO wipe guard here, so an empty string is accepted and clears the SOP, and a fragment silently replaces everything else. Both answer 200. Read the current SOP first and fold your change into it. Omit the field to leave it alone.
sop_md.title: Sop Md

tools.name: update_task_manual

tools.description: Delete a task type (open tasks of the type → 409).
tools.name: delete_task_manual

tools.description: Whole-doc replace of a type's learnings (task-close write-back). The doc text goes in text (NOT learnings — that is update_task_manual's field name); text is REQUIRED and unknown keys are rejected. Wiping existing learnings needs allow_shrink=true.

text.title: Text
text.description: The ENTIRE learnings doc, not an addition to it: whatever you send becomes the whole document and everything else is gone. The field name says 'text' but the seam is a whole-doc replace, so sending the paragraph you wanted to add answers 200 and permanently drops the rest. Read the current doc first and send it back with your change folded in, or use patch_task_learnings, which edits by anchor instead. TWO guards stand here and they behave differently. The wipe guard catches only the extreme case - emptying a doc that had content - and allow_shrink=true switches it off; either way, a replace that merely loses most of the text passes without comment. The second is the learnings size cap, and it is UNCONDITIONAL: allow_shrink is not a bypass for it, it refuses any text over the cap that is not shorter than what is stored, and its refusal names your length, the cap and the current length. Note the sibling update_task_manual writes this same document through its 'learnings' field: it enforces the same cap, but it has NO wipe guard, so an empty string sent there erases the doc without asking.

tools.name: write_task_learnings

tools.description: Patch a type's learnings by unique anchors ({edits:[{old,new}]}) — the learnings twin of patch_lessons, so the write cost scales with the CHANGE, not the whole (30k-char) doc, and re-typing the whole doc can no longer silently drop content. Edits apply in order; a non-empty old must match the current learnings EXACTLY ONCE (0 or >1 hits reject the WHOLE batch with a 400, zero writes — the unique anchor also acts as an optimistic lock); an empty old appends. Wiping the doc, or shrinking it below a tenth, needs allow_shrink=true.
tools.name: patch_task_learnings

tools.description: Patch a type's SOP (sop_md) by unique anchors ({edits:[{old,new}]}) — send only the section that changed, instead of re-typing the whole SOP. USE THIS WHENEVER YOU ARE AMENDING AN SOP THAT ALREADY HAS CONTENT. update_task_manual{sop_md} is a wholesale replace, so if anyone else edited the SOP between your read and your write, your copy is stale and the replace silently deletes their section — and because your stale copy is usually the LONGER one, no guard fires and nothing tells you. A patch cannot do that: a non-empty old must match the current sop_md EXACTLY ONCE (0 or >1 hits reject the WHOLE batch with a 400 that names which edit failed and which tool to re-read with, zero writes), so a concurrent write turns into a refusal you can see. Edits apply in order; an empty old appends. Wiping the doc, or shrinking it below a tenth, needs allow_shrink=true — for an honest rewrite from scratch use update_task_manual. The sop_md cap is judged on the RESULT and allow_shrink is not a bypass. Re-read with get_task_manual after a refusal.
tools.name: patch_task_sop

tools.description:
READ the CATALOGUE of retained versions of one editable document: which versions exist, when each was replaced and by whom, whether each was a tombstone, and HOW LONG each of its fields was. It does NOT carry the versions themselves — a version list is how you CHOOSE one, and choosing does not need the prose; fetch the one you picked with get_document_version. Read-only, newest first, and only the most recent few are kept — HOW MANY is per-document and is not stated here, because it differs by kind and this sentence would go stale silently; what you get back is the answer. Putting a version BACK is deliberately not an agent tool — the owner does that from the cockpit — so this cannot change anything.

WHICH DOCUMENTS THIS COVERS, AND WHAT `key` LOOKS LIKE FOR EACH, ARE DELIBERATELY NOT LISTED HERE. A list of kinds — or of key shapes — written into a description goes stale the moment a new editable document ships, and NOTHING turns red when it does: this description used to enumerate six kinds and a key shape per kind, and both had already gone stale before the lists were taken out. Two rules you can actually execute replace them.

ADDRESSING: `kind` and `key` are validated by the same server-side gate that answers get_document_seed, so whatever that tool can address, this one can too, and the two can never silently disagree. A `kind` this server does not know is refused with 400; a retired kind is refused with 400 naming the series that replaced it. Some kinds also police the shape of `key` before answering — a key this kind does not serve, or one that fails that kind's required shape, is refused with 400 naming the problem. Neither is something to guess at: ask and read the answer.

COVERAGE: a syntactically valid `key` that simply has no retained versions yet is not an error — it returns an empty list, the honest 'nothing has been saved here', not a gap to work around.

key.description: Which document of that kind to list revisions for. How strictly it is checked depends entirely on kind, so an empty list means different things in different places. For system_interaction and boot_sequence, a key this server does not serve is 400 and the message names the legal key(s). For lessons the key is 'role_key::task_type' and anything without both halves is 400 - but that is the ONLY check it gets: past the split nothing looks the bucket up (the one remaining gate there is a WRITE authorisation, which a list never reaches), so a well-formed name for a bucket nobody has ever written, 'r-nobody::typo', is 200 with an EMPTY list. The retired kind task_manual is 400 whatever the key, naming task_manual_sop and task_manual_learnings instead. For every REMAINING kind - global_context, role_definition, insight, the two task_manual series, task_description, task_title - the value is used as a plain equality condition and nothing checks that it names anything, so a key that names no document answers 200 with an EMPTY list too. That is the same answer a real document with no retained revisions gives, so on lessons and on all of those an empty list cannot tell you 'this document has never been edited' apart from 'you named it wrong'; only system_interaction, boot_sequence and the retired task_manual are loud about a WELL-FORMED name that points at nothing. A MALFORMED lessons key - one missing its '::' - is 400 and never reaches the empty list at all.

tools.description:
READ the SHIPPED DEFAULT of one editable document — the text a reset would put back, i.e. the 初始版本 entry of that document's version list. Read-only: this tool writes nothing, so reading the default can never replace the live document. Putting the default BACK is deliberately not an agent tool — the owner does that from the cockpit — exactly as with list_document_history. ``content`` carries the SAME field names a retained version carries, so the same reader can compare a default against the live document.

WHICH DOCUMENTS THIS COVERS IS DELIBERATELY NOT LISTED HERE. A list of kinds written into a description goes stale the moment a new editable document ships and NOTHING turns red when it does — this one had gone wrong about three kinds before the list was taken out. Two rules you can actually execute replace it.

ADDRESSING: ``kind`` and ``key`` name a document exactly as they do for list_document_history — the same server-side gate answers both routes, so whatever that tool addresses is addressable here, and a ``kind`` this server does not know is refused with 400 while a ``key`` that names no document of that kind is refused with 404 that names it. Neither is something to guess at: ask and read the answer.

COVERAGE: whether THAT document ships a default is answered by asking for it. 200 means it does, and ``content`` is that text. 404 means it has none at all — a role the owner created, a task manual, per-role lessons — which is the same set whose reset the server also 404s, so it is the honest 'there is nothing to go back to', not a gap to work around. 400 on a retired kind names the series that replaced it.

key.description: Which document of that kind to fetch the shipped default for. For most kinds a key nothing carries answers 404 and names it, so the mistake surfaces - but kind=global_context is the exception: there the key is NEVER READ. Any non-empty key answers 200 with the one global-context seed, so a caller who asked for a specific document gets a document that has nothing to do with the name it asked for, and the response echoes the key back as though it had been honoured. When the kind is global_context, do not read the key you sent as evidence of what you received.

tools.name: get_document_seed

tools.description:
READ the BODY of one named retained version of an editable document — the ``content`` map that version was stored with, exactly as it was stored. Read-only: this fetches text, it never puts it back; restoring stays out of the agent tool surface, as it does for list_document_history.

THIS IS THE SECOND HALF OF A PAIR. list_document_history answers WHICH versions exist and how big each field of each one is, and carries no prose at all; this answers WHAT ONE OF THEM SAID. Name the ``id`` you read off that list. Asking for every version's text is the cost that pairing exists to remove, so fetch the one you actually mean to read.

ADDRESSING: ``kind`` and ``key`` name a document exactly as they do for list_document_history — the same server-side gate answers all three routes, so whatever that tool can address, this one can too, and they can never silently disagree. A ``kind`` this server does not know is refused with 400; a retired kind is refused with 400 naming the series that replaced it; a ``key`` that fails its kind's required shape is refused with 400 naming the problem. An ``id`` that is not a retained version of THAT document is a 404 — including an id that belongs to some other document, which is why the address is the whole triple and not the id alone.

id.description: WHICH retained version to read, as the id list_document_history reported for it. It is scoped to the kind/key pair you also send: an id that names a version of a DIFFERENT document is a 404, not that other document's text.

key.description: Which document of that kind the version belongs to - addressed exactly as list_document_history addresses it, by the same server-side gate.
